periods.activity_title: Mapping the Five Spheres and Tracing Disturbances Across Them
periods.visual_aids: Textbook landscape diagram showing geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere

time_bands.activity: Students examine the textbook landscape diagram and individually identify one concrete example from each of the five spheres, writing their answers on the blank chart. The teacher then collects two or three responses for each sphere on the board without evaluation.

Working in pairs, students trace the journey of snow from the cryosphere into the hydrosphere as lake water, annotating arrows on their chart. They then reason: if snowfall in a mountain region decreases, what chain of effects moves through the five spheres? Each pair records at least three sphere-to-sphere links.

Pairs share their disturbance chains with another pair, comparing similarities and differences. The class pool of chains is collected on the board, and the teacher facilitates a brief discussion identifying which sphere-to-sphere links appeared most often and why.

Students individually write two sentences: one naming the sphere where the disturbance begins and one explaining why the effect does not stop at one sphere. The teacher reads three or four aloud to close the discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's core framing — the idea that Earth functions as a system of five interacting spheres. Watch for students who treat the spheres as completely separate compartments and believe a change in one sphere has no bearing on the others; the snow-to-lake-water trace is the most direct way to challenge that view. A useful checkpoint: if most pairs can name at least two downstream sphere effects from reduced snowfall, they are ready to move to the chapter's content on energy inputs.

periods.activity_title: Solar Radiation, Albedo, and Why Surfaces Heat Unevenly
periods.section_anchor: 13.1 Uneven Heating of the Earth / 13.1.1 Interaction of solar radiation on the Earth's surface
materials: Albedo reference table (Activity 13.2 values: snow, ice, crushed rock, light soil, black soil, ocean water)
Graph paper or squared notebook page
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of the electromagnetic spectrum showing UV, visible, and IR bands with approximate wavelength ranges and Earth-surface interactions

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws the EM spectrum on the board, marking UV, visible, and IR regions. Students label what happens to each band: UV absorbed by ozone, visible light drives photosynthesis and warms surfaces, IR warms the surface and is partly re-radiated. The solar constant value (1.4 kWm⁻²) and maximum surface insolation (1 kWm⁻²) are recorded with the teacher explaining why atmospheric absorption accounts for the difference.

Students complete the albedo table from Activity 13.2 using textbook values (snow 0.80–0.90, ice 0.50–0.70, black soil low, ocean water low). They then construct a simple bar sketch ranking the six surfaces from highest to lowest albedo, and write one sentence explaining why polar regions remain very cold. The teacher circulates, checking that students connect high albedo to more reflection and therefore lower surface warming.

The teacher introduces the urban heat island effect using the contrast between dark asphalt/concrete and forest or vegetation. Students annotate a simple city-versus-rural cross-section sketch on their page, labelling which surfaces absorb more, which re-radiate heat at night, and why cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas during summer evenings.

Quick whole-class check: the teacher names a surface and students call out whether its albedo is high or low and whether the surface will be warmer or cooler. Three or four surfaces are enough to confirm understanding before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that the Earth system receives unequal energy through solar radiation, this unit grounds the mechanism — how surface properties determine how much energy is absorbed versus reflected. A frequent confusion is that dark surfaces are simply 'hotter by nature' rather than because they absorb more radiation; the albedo concept directly corrects this. Asking students to predict whether a black-soil field or a snow-covered field will be warmer on a sunny afternoon is a useful probing question.
homework: Using the albedo values from today's table, explain in two or three sentences why a city's night-time temperature might remain higher than a forested area even after the sun has set.

periods.activity_title: Latitude, Earth's Shape, and Atmospheric Layers as Climate Drivers
materials: Torch or phone flashlight (one per group of four)
Two sheets of white paper per group
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing a spherical Earth with parallel solar rays striking equatorial and polar regions at different angles

time_bands.activity: In groups of four, students shine a torch perpendicular to a flat sheet of paper and trace the lit oval on the page. They then tilt the paper at roughly 45° and trace the new, larger oval. Both ovals are from the same torch — same energy — but spread over different areas. Students measure the two ovals and record the ratio of areas, discovering that tilted surfaces receive lower energy per unit area.

Groups connect their torch observation to Earth's geometry: the teacher draws parallel solar rays hitting a spherical Earth on the board. Students explain in their notebooks why equatorial regions are warmer than polar regions, referencing both the angle of incidence and the area over which the same solar energy spreads. They extend this to explain seasons and why the North Pole experiences months of darkness.

The teacher briefly presents the temperature-gradient consequence: the equator-to-pole temperature difference creates a pressure gradient that is the primary driver of global atmospheric circulation and ocean currents. Students note this link between geometry, temperature, and circulation as a key causal chain in their notebooks, in their own words.
Each student writes one causal sentence connecting Earth's spherical shape to global wind circulation, without using the word 'because' — forcing them to use a mechanism rather than a label.

periods.teacher_notes: The torch-and-paper activity makes the geometric argument physically concrete before it is treated abstractly. A common error is that students think polar regions are cold simply because they are 'far from the Sun' rather than because the same energy spreads over a larger area due to the angle; the measurement of the two ovals directly addresses this. If groups finish early, ask them to predict what would happen to Earth's temperature gradients if the planet were flat.

periods.activity_title: From Pressure Gradients to Local and Planetary Wind Systems
periods.section_anchor: 13.2 Uneven Heating Causes Wind and Ocean Currents
materials: Blank world map outline (one per student)
Coloured pencils (two colours for warm and cold currents)
periods.visual_aids: Board sketch of valley-breeze and mountain-breeze daytime versus night-time flow; board diagram of three-cell global circulation with pressure belt labels

time_bands.activity: Students read the valley and mountain breeze description and draw a two-panel diagram in their notebooks: one for daytime (valley breeze) and one for night-time (mountain breeze), labelling which surface heats or cools faster and drawing arrows for air movement. The teacher then draws the same on the board and students self-check their arrows.

The teacher guides students through the three-pressure-belt planetary circulation model on the board: equatorial low, subtropical high, sub-polar low, polar high. Students annotate a copy of the board sketch in their notebooks, tracing air rising and sinking and labelling wind direction. The teacher introduces Earth's rotation causing rightward deflection in the Northern Hemisphere as an additional factor students note but do not need to calculate.

Students complete their blank world map by drawing and labelling the major ocean gyres: clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, counter-clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. They mark the North Atlantic Drift, label it as an extension of the Gulf Stream, and write one sentence explaining why it keeps north-western European ports ice-free at high latitudes.

Three or four students share their maps, and the class discusses whether the same principle — differential heating creating pressure gradients that drive flow — operates at both the valley-breeze and the planetary-wind scale. Students note the answer in one sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: The uneven heating established in sections 13.1 and 13.1.2 finds its direct consequence here — pressure gradients driving wind and water movement. Students often assume wind always blows from cold to hot; the pressure-gradient framing (high to low pressure) prevents this error. Checking that students can correctly reverse the mountain-breeze arrow direction between daytime and night-time is a reliable indicator they have understood the mechanism rather than memorised a label.
homework: On your world-map sketch, add arrows showing where warm equatorial surface water moves and where it eventually sinks as it cools near the poles. Write two sentences explaining how this pattern affects the climate of a region the current reaches.

periods.activity_title: Tracing the Water Cycle and Its Climate-Change Disruptions
materials: News excerpt or teacher-prepared data: two contrasting scenarios — glacial melt adding to river flow versus drought-affected groundwater decline
periods.visual_aids: Board sketch of the water cycle showing evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff, and infiltration with sphere labels

time_bands.activity: Students individually draw the water cycle from memory on blank paper, labelling every process they can recall: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration. The teacher then shows the board sketch; students add any missing labels in a different colour so they can see what they independently recalled versus what needed prompting.

The teacher presents the two contrasting scenarios from the news excerpt: heavy rainfall and flooding in one region, prolonged drought and groundwater depletion in another. In pairs, students annotate their water-cycle diagrams to show which parts of the cycle are intensified in each scenario, linking each change to a warmer atmosphere holding more moisture. They label which Earth spheres are affected in each scenario.

Each pair joins another pair to compare annotations. Groups reconcile any differences and jointly identify one effect on agriculture and one effect on coastal cities (Mumbai or Chennai) from the disrupted water cycle, drawing on the section's reference to glacier melt raising sea levels and intense rainfall increasing surface runoff while reducing groundwater recharge.

One spokesperson per group of four shares their coastal city effect with the class. The teacher notes the sphere-to-sphere links on the board, confirming that cryosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere, and biosphere all appear in the group's chains.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit grounds the abstract water cycle in the concrete consequences of climate-change intensification — heavier rains in some areas, drought elsewhere, glacier melt raising sea levels. Watch for students who think the water cycle speeds up uniformly with warming; the contrasting scenarios are designed to show that intensification is uneven across regions. If groups are struggling to link glacier melt to coastal flooding, ask them to trace where the meltwater goes step by step.

periods.activity_title: Nitrogen Cycle: Microbial Conversions That Sustain All Life
materials: Five role-labels (sticky notes or folded card): N₂ in atmosphere, NH₃ in soil, NO₂⁻ in soil, NO₃⁻ in soil, organic N in organisms
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of the full nitrogen cycle with named bacteria at each conversion step

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a simple circle on the board labelled 'Atmosphere: N₂' and asks: 'Plants need nitrogen to make proteins. Is atmospheric N₂ directly available to plants?' Students respond, and the teacher uses their answers to establish the core problem — N₂ is non-reactive — before introducing the idea that bacteria solve it.

The teacher builds the nitrogen cycle on the board step by step, naming each bacterium as its conversion is drawn: Rhizobium (nodules) and Azotobacter (soil) fix N₂ to NH₃; Nitrosomonas converts NH₃ to NO₂⁻; Nitrobacter converts NO₂⁻ to NO₃⁻; plants absorb NO₃⁻; animals eat plants; decomposers return NH₃ through ammonification; Pseudomonas carries out denitrification back to N₂. Students copy the diagram with all labels.

Five volunteers each hold a role-label (N₂, NH₃, NO₂⁻, NO₃⁻, organic N) and stand in a circle at the front. The rest of the class directs them to move clockwise or call out which bacterium performs the transition between each pair of volunteers, using their notebooks. The teacher corrects errors in real time and repeats any step where direction is uncertain.

Students write the nitrogen cycle as a linear conversion sequence using arrows and chemical formulas only: N₂ → NH₃ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ → organic N → NH₃ → N₂, placing the bacterium name above each arrow. This compact notation becomes their summary.

periods.teacher_notes: The nitrogen cycle is dense with bacterial names and chemical forms, and students frequently confuse the direction of nitrification (NH₃ to nitrate) with denitrification (nitrate back to N₂); building the cycle step by step on the board, rather than presenting it complete, reduces this confusion. The standing-circle role-play is specifically designed to make the conversion sequence a physical experience rather than a visual memorisation task. If time is tight, the role-play can run with just four students covering the four inorganic forms.
homework: Write three sentences explaining why a legume crop such as lentils or soybeans can improve soil fertility for a following crop — name the specific bacterium and chemical conversion involved.

periods.activity_title: Human Disruption of Earth's Cycles: Evidence, Mechanisms, and Responses
materials: Board or projected data: atmospheric CO₂ rise from 315 ppm (1960) to 420 ppm (present), approximately 35% increase
periods.visual_aids: Board table listing human activity, disrupted cycle, mechanism, and one observed consequence — four rows: fossil fuel combustion, nitrogen fertiliser overuse, deforestation, vehicular emissions

time_bands.activity: The teacher presents the CO₂ data (315 ppm to 420 ppm since 1960) and asks students to calculate the percentage increase, confirming the approximately 35% figure. Students identify this as evidence of human disruption of the carbon cycle, linking it to fossil fuel combustion and deforestation reducing photosynthesis and transpiration.

The teacher builds the four-row disruption table on the board collaboratively with the class: students provide the mechanism and consequence for each human activity based on their reading, and the teacher supplements or corrects. Eutrophication (excess nitrates → algal bloom → oxygen depletion → fish death) receives special attention because students often think fertilisers only help plants and are surprised by the aquatic harm.

Students evaluate two international responses — the Montreal Protocol (ozone, largely successful) and the Paris Agreement (CO₂, less effective) — and write a structured comparison in their notebooks: what each agreement targets, what evidence suggests about its effectiveness, and one reason why the CO₂ effort has been harder. They draw on section 13.4's content rather than outside knowledge.

Each student writes one specific individual or community action from section 13.4 and traces how it would slow one particular disruption identified in the table, naming the cycle, the mechanism, and the sphere most directly relieved. Three students share aloud to close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to evaluate human disruption mechanisms and policy responses — a shift from description to analysis. A common gap is treating eutrophication as a direct nitrogen-poisoning of fish rather than understanding the oxygen-depletion mechanism via algal blooms; the table construction step is designed to make the mechanism explicit. Asking students to explain why the Montreal Protocol succeeded while CO₂ efforts have not is a strong probing question that draws on the difference between a single chemical cause (CFCs) and a globally embedded energy system.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can trace how a disturbance introduced into one component of an interconnected system propagates to affect other components.
questions.section_context: Five Earth spheres — geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere, biosphere — and sphere-to-sphere disturbance propagation

competency.competency_text: Analyse how energy and matter flow across the Earth's interconnected spheres and how human disruption of these flows cascades across ecosystems.

questions.question_text: A prolonged drought in a mountain region causes the glaciers there to shrink significantly. Which sequence correctly traces how this cryosphere change propagates to the biosphere?

options.label: A
options.text: Smaller glaciers → higher ocean salinity (hydrosphere) → reduced evaporation → drought ends before reaching biosphere

options.label: B
options.text: Smaller glaciers → increased atmospheric nitrogen (atmosphere) → faster plant growth (biosphere) → higher river flow (hydrosphere)

options.label: C
options.text: Smaller glaciers → less meltwater entering rivers (hydrosphere) → lower river flow → reduced water available to riverside vegetation and animals (biosphere)

options.label: D
options.text: Smaller glaciers → more sunlight reflected from exposed rock (geosphere) → cooler atmosphere → expanded biosphere habitat

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses sphere identity — links glacial shrinkage to atmospheric nitrogen rather than water flow, showing a failure to trace matter through the correct sphere pathway.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Partially correct about exposed rock reflecting more light but then inverts the warming effect and incorrectly concludes the biosphere expands rather than being stressed.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates local glacier melt with ocean salinity changes and inverts causation, showing a misconception that the system self-corrects automatically before effects reach living organisms.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the full chain may still demonstrate partial understanding by correctly identifying the first or second sphere-to-sphere link; probe with follow-up oral questions to distinguish partial from complete grasp.

questions.question_text: A city neighbourhood replaces a large park with a concrete parking lot. Which prediction about surface temperature in that neighbourhood is best supported by the concept of albedo?

options.label: A
options.text: Daytime temperature will rise but night-time temperature will fall, because concrete stops absorbing energy once the sun sets.

options.label: B
options.text: Temperature will remain unchanged because the total solar radiation arriving in the neighbourhood does not change when vegetation is removed.

options.label: C
options.text: The neighbourhood will become cooler, because the concrete surface reflects more solar radiation than the dark soil under the park.

options.label: D
options.text: The neighbourhood will become warmer during the day and remain warmer at night, because concrete has lower albedo than vegetation and absorbs and retains more solar radiation.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Incorrectly assigns high albedo to concrete — confuses light-coloured versus dark-coloured surfaces, or recalls that high albedo means cooler without knowing that concrete has lower albedo than vegetated surfaces.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Correctly identifies daytime warming but misunderstands heat retention — does not recognise that concrete re-radiates stored heat at night, the core mechanism of the urban heat island effect.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Treats albedo as irrelevant and focuses only on incoming radiation — a recall failure to connect surface properties to the fraction of energy absorbed.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who cannot articulate the full albedo mechanism may still demonstrate understanding of the direction of change (warmer) even without naming albedo; credit partial reasoning and ask a follow-up to elicit the mechanism.

questions.question_text: Two identical beams of solar radiation — each carrying the same total energy — arrive at Earth's surface simultaneously. Beam X strikes the equatorial region nearly perpendicular to the surface. Beam Y strikes a polar region at a shallow angle. Explain why the surface temperature produced by Beam Y is lower than that produced by Beam X, using the concept of energy distribution over area. Then state one consequence of this temperature difference for global atmospheric circulation.
expected_elements: Beam Y strikes at a shallow angle, so the same energy is spread over a larger surface area than Beam X.
Energy per unit area (intensity) at the polar surface is therefore lower than at the equatorial surface.
Lower intensity means less energy available to heat each unit of the polar surface, resulting in a lower surface temperature.

The equator-to-pole temperature difference creates a pressure gradient (warm equatorial air rises, creating low pressure; cold polar air sinks, creating high pressure) that drives global atmospheric circulation / planetary winds.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who can correctly explain the area-spread mechanism but cannot articulate the circulation consequence still demonstrate the core geometric reasoning; award partial credit and probe the circulation link verbally. Students who draw diagrams to support their explanation should receive equal credit to those who write prose.

questions.question_text: In a Himalayan valley, a farmer notices that a cool breeze blows down from the mountain slopes into the valley after sunset each evening. Which explanation correctly identifies the mechanism responsible for this breeze?

options.label: A
options.text: After sunset, both slopes and valley cool at the same rate, so the breeze is driven by the higher altitude of the slopes creating a natural gravitational pull on air.

options.label: B
options.text: After sunset, mountain slopes cool faster than the valley floor, making the air over the slopes cooler and denser; this denser air flows downhill into the valley as a mountain breeze.

options.label: C
options.text: After sunset, the valley floor cools faster than the slopes, making valley air denser; this denser valley air rises and draws slope air down as a replacement flow.

options.label: D
options.text: After sunset, warm air trapped in the valley rises to fill the space left by cooling slope air, creating an uphill breeze rather than a downhill one.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Inverts the relative cooling rates — assigns faster cooling to the valley floor rather than the slopes, showing a confusion between the day and night surface-heating pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Replaces the differential-cooling mechanism with a gravitational-altitude explanation, indicating a recall failure to connect the pressure-gradient principle to this specific local wind.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Correctly identifies that warm air rises but applies the daytime (valley breeze) logic to the night-time situation, showing a confusion between which direction the breezes run and when.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who can correctly identify that slopes cool faster but cannot explain the density-driven flow mechanism still demonstrate the key observation; follow up to elicit the pressure-gradient link orally.

competency.competency_text: Analyse how energy and matter flow across the Earth's interconnected spheres and how human disruption of these flows cascades across ecosystems.

questions.question_text: Global average temperatures have risen steadily over the past century. A climate scientist states: 'A warmer atmosphere does not simply speed up the water cycle uniformly — it produces opposite effects in different parts of the world and within the same cycle.' Using specific stages of the water cycle and named consequences from the chapter, analyse how this statement is supported by evidence. Your response should address at least two contrasting regional or stage-level effects.
look_for: Identifies that a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, intensifying evaporation and leading to heavier precipitation events in some regions.

Identifies that the same warming causes accelerated glacier melt, adding water to rivers initially but threatening long-term freshwater supply, and raising sea levels threatening coastal cities such as Mumbai or Chennai.
Identifies the contrast: some regions experience flooding from intense rainfall while others face drought as precipitation shifts geographically.
Identifies that intense rainfall increases surface runoff while reducing infiltration and groundwater recharge, making water unavailable for agriculture even during heavy rain events.
Links at least two contrasting effects explicitly to different stages or different regions of the water cycle, demonstrating that disruption is non-uniform rather than a simple speed-up.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who provide only one contrasting effect still demonstrate partial analysis; award partial credit and probe for the second contrast verbally. Students who express their reasoning through annotated diagrams of the water cycle rather than prose should receive equal consideration — the diagram must show the contrasting effects explicitly labelled to earn full credit.

questions.question_text: A farmer plants a legume crop (such as lentils) in a field and, after harvesting, leaves the roots in the soil. The following season, a non-legume crop grown in the same field shows better growth than usual without any added fertiliser. Using the nitrogen cycle, explain the mechanism responsible for the improved growth. Name the specific bacterium and chemical conversion involved.
expected_elements: Legume roots host Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules.
Rhizobium fixes atmospheric N₂ into ammonia (NH₃), which enters the soil when roots decompose.
Nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter) convert NH₃ first to nitrite (NO₂⁻) then to nitrate (NO₃⁻) in the soil.
The non-legume crop absorbs NO₃⁻ from the soil through its roots to synthesise proteins and nucleic acids, explaining improved growth.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who correctly name Rhizobium and nitrogen fixation but omit the nitrification steps still demonstrate partial cycle knowledge; probe for the conversion to nitrate. Students who draw the relevant portion of the nitrogen cycle with labelled arrows may substitute that diagram for prose and should receive equal credit.

competency.competency_text: Analyse how energy and matter flow across the Earth's interconnected spheres and how human disruption of these flows cascades across ecosystems.

questions.visual_stimulus:
Policy | Target substance | Year of adoption | Measurable outcome by 2020
Montreal Protocol | CFCs (ozone-depleting chemicals) | 1987 | Ozone hole showing measurable recovery; CFC concentrations declining
Kyoto Protocol | CO₂ and other greenhouse gases | 1997 | CO₂ concentrations continued rising; limited binding commitments
Paris Agreement | CO₂ and other greenhouse gases | 2015 | Global CO₂ rose from ~400 ppm (2015) to ~420 ppm (2023); commitments voluntary
questions.task: The table above shows three international environmental agreements, their target substances, and measurable outcomes. Using the data in the table and your knowledge of how human activities disrupt Earth's cycles, evaluate why the Montreal Protocol has been more effective than the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement in reversing the disruption it addressed. Then identify one specific individual or community action that addresses a different disruption covered in this chapter, and explain which Earth sphere it most directly relieves and through which mechanism.
questions.scaffold: Part 1 — Comparing effectiveness (refer to the table): What did each agreement target? What does the measurable outcome column tell you about whether the disruption has been reversed? Why might targeting a single industrial chemical be more tractable than targeting CO₂? Part 2 — Individual or community action: Name one action from the chapter. State which cycle disruption it addresses, which sphere is most directly relieved, and what the mechanism of relief is.
format_of_output: Part 1: A written evaluation of 3–5 sentences comparing the Montreal Protocol with at least one CO₂ agreement, using specific data from the table.
Part 2: A written explanation of 2–3 sentences naming the action, the disruption it addresses, the sphere relieved, and the mechanism.

OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The section's implied_lo requires evaluating a response measure against evidence of change — a data table providing policy outcomes is the most direct vehicle for that evaluation, avoiding the need to rely on outside knowledge.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can read measurable-outcome data to judge the effectiveness of a policy intervention, connect that effectiveness to the specificity of the mechanism targeted, and then apply the same analytical logic to a different disruption-response pair from the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Part 1 prompts guide students to read the table column by column before synthesising; Part 2 asks for a concrete chapter-grounded example rather than a general claim. A strong response to Part 1 references specific ppm figures or the 'showing measurable recovery' entry; a weak one makes general statements without citing the table data.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: cites specific data from the table (CFC decline and ozone recovery versus continued CO₂ rise to 420 ppm); explains that CFCs were a single class of industrial chemicals with clear substitutes, while CO₂ is embedded in energy systems globally; names a specific action in Part 2 with a mechanistic sphere-level explanation. Weak: makes general claims that 'Montreal worked better' without citing the table; lists an action in Part 2 without identifying the mechanism or sphere.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the comparative evaluation may still demonstrate partial understanding by correctly reading the table outcome for one agreement; probe Part 2 separately. Students who prefer to respond with an annotated version of the table plus brief notes rather than prose paragraphs should receive equal credit provided the evaluation and mechanism are explicit.
